lessons.title: Extrinsic Factors Affecting Injury Risk
lessons.description: How type of activity, coaching, environment and equipment shape the risk and severity of sports injuries.
lessons.content_html:
What Are Extrinsic Factors?

Not every sports injury can be blamed on the athlete. Extrinsic factors are influences in the athlete's external environment — the type of sport they play, the quality of coaching they receive, the surface they perform on, and the equipment they wear. Understanding each factor is essential because examiners regularly ask you to apply them to real sporting scenarios and to explain how they interact with one another.

Type of Sporting Activity

The nature of a sport is the starting point for risk assessment. High-contact sports such as rugby union or ice hockey carry a higher probability of traumatic injuries — fractures, dislocations and concussion — because direct physical collision is a core part of play. Individual precision sports such as golf or archery carry a much lower collision risk but can still produce overuse injuries if technique is poor or training loads are excessive. Water-based activities introduce the unique risk of drowning and hypothermia, while winter sports on snow and ice raise the likelihood of high-speed falls. When comparing activities, consider contact level, speed of movement, use of implements, and the natural environment involved.

Key Fact

High-contact sports (e.g. rugby, ice hockey) are associated with acute traumatic injuries such as fractures and concussion, whereas non-contact or precision sports are more commonly linked to chronic overuse injuries if training loads are poorly managed.

Coaching, Instruction and Leadership

A coach is one of the most powerful protective factors in sport — or, when provision is poor, one of the greatest risk factors. Five key elements are identified. Knowledge of techniques, rules and regulations ensures athletes are taught safe movement patterns from the outset. Experience allows a coach to spot early signs of fatigue or poor technique that a novice coach might miss. Clear communication means that instructions about correct warm-up, equipment use and safe landing technique are actually understood. Supervision ensures athletes are never left to practise dangerous skills unsupervised. Finally, ethical standards — including not pressurising athletes to play through pain — protect long-term health. A coach who lacks experience and fails to supervise correctly multiplies injury risk significantly.

Environment

The environment an athlete competes or trains in has three dimensions: weather and temperature conditions, the playing surface and surrounding area, and human interaction. Extreme heat increases the risk of heat exhaustion and dehydration; extreme cold raises the likelihood of muscle strains because cold muscles have reduced elasticity. Wet or icy conditions reduce surface traction, dramatically increasing the chance of slips and falls. Playing surface matters greatly: a waterlogged grass pitch increases the chance of ankle sprains, while an excessively hard artificial surface increases ground-reaction forces on joints, raising the risk of stress fractures and shin splints. Human interaction — other performers, officials and spectators — also plays a role. Opponents who play dangerously or illegally raise contact injury risk; officials who fail to enforce rules allow dangerous play to continue; hostile crowds can increase performer anxiety, which in turn can lead to reckless play and injury.

The spec explicitly links playing surface with appropriate footwear as an example of how extrinsic factors interact. A footballer wearing long metal studs on an artificial 3G surface will find the studs catching rather than releasing, placing enormous rotational stress on the knee — increasing the risk of an ACL sprain. Wearing moulded rubber studs designed for artificial turf reduces this risk. Similarly, a cross-country runner wearing road-running shoes on muddy terrain lacks the grip needed to prevent ankle inversion, so appropriate footwear choice is always surface-dependent. In exam answers, linking surface type to footwear selection will consistently earn higher marks.

Equipment

Protective equipment is specifically designed to reduce both the likelihood and severity of injury. A cyclist wearing a correctly fitted helmet significantly reduces the severity of any head impact; shin guards in football reduce the severity of direct blows to the tibia. Performance equipment — bats, rackets, bikes, poles — must be correctly fitted and in good condition; a cracked hockey stick or a poorly fitted bicycle saddle can alter biomechanics and lead to overuse injury. Clothing appropriate for the conditions (thermal layers in cold, breathable fabrics in heat) helps regulate body temperature and prevents environmental medical conditions. Footwear is arguably the single most important piece of equipment for injury prevention: it must provide appropriate cushioning, support and grip for the specific surface and activity.

Key Fact

Protective equipment reduces both injury likelihood and severity — for example, a correctly fitted mouthguard significantly reduces the risk of dental and jaw injuries in contact sports, while appropriate footwear reduces the risk of ankle sprains by providing surface-specific grip and lateral support.

Officials are part of the human interaction element of the environment. A referee who strictly enforces rules about dangerous tackles, illegal contact or unsafe play directly reduces the chance of traumatic injuries occurring. Conversely, a permissive official who allows high tackles in rugby or dangerous challenges in football creates an environment where athletes are more likely to be injured. The spec asks you to understand that officials and spectators are part of the environment — they are not passive bystanders but active contributors to risk level. Linking official behaviour to coaching and type of activity in extended answers demonstrates the synoptic thinking OCR rewards.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For 6- and 8-mark questions on extrinsic factors, the highest marks go to answers that show how factors interact — not just list them. For example: an icy playing surface means that footwear with insufficient grip significantly increases fall risk, and a coach without experience who does not recognise these hazards compounds the danger. Always use a named sport or specific scenario as your example, and use the precise spec language: "playing surface", "protective equipment", "coaching/instructing/leading" rather than informal alternatives.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The four extrinsic factors — type of sporting activity, coaching/instruction, environment (weather, surface, human interaction), and equipment (protective, performance, clothing, footwear) — all influence injury risk and severity, and they interact with one another.
  • Coaching quality is both a risk factor and a protective factor: a knowledgeable, experienced coach who communicates well and supervises correctly can significantly reduce the impact of other extrinsic hazards.
  • High marks come from linking extrinsic factors together (e.g. surface type determining footwear choice) and applying them to named sporting scenarios rather than describing each factor in isolation.

A grassroots football club trains on a waterlogged grass pitch in winter. The coach has limited experience and the players wear summer moulded boots.

lessons.title: Intrinsic Factors Affecting Injury Risk
lessons.description: How individual variables and psychological factors within the athlete influence their risk and severity of injury.
lessons.content_html:
What Are Intrinsic Factors?

Intrinsic factors are the internal characteristics that the athlete brings to every session — their age, fitness, nutrition, sleep quality, psychological state and injury history. Unlike extrinsic factors, intrinsic factors cannot always be controlled by a coach or facility manager; they require the athlete themselves to take responsibility for their own preparation and wellbeing. Intrinsic factors divide into individual variables and psychological factors.

Individual Variables

The specification lists ten individual variables. Gender influences injury risk because anatomical differences — including hip width, hormonal fluctuations and average muscle mass — mean that female athletes are statistically more susceptible to ACL injuries, while male athletes are more often involved in high-contact traumatic events. Age affects risk in both directions: younger athletes have developing bones and growth plates that are vulnerable to fracture and overuse; older athletes have reduced muscle elasticity, slower recovery rates and often longer histories of accumulated joint stress. Experience and technique/ability are closely related — poor technique places abnormal stress on muscles, tendons and joints, raising overuse and acute injury risk. Weight affects the load placed through joints on every step or landing; excessive body mass increases ground-reaction forces through the knees and hips, raising the risk of chronic conditions such as patellar tendonitis and shin splints.

Fitness levels interact with weight — a high fitness level means muscles, tendons and ligaments are better conditioned to withstand the demands of sport. Nutrition and hydration directly support muscle repair, bone density and energy availability; a poorly nourished athlete fatigues earlier and is more prone to both acute and chronic injury. Sleep is when the body repairs damaged tissue; chronic sleep deprivation impairs reaction time, coordination and pain tolerance, all of which elevate injury risk. Medical conditions — such as asthma, diabetes or a known cardiovascular issue — may limit the type or intensity of activity that is safe. Finally, previous or recurring injuries are one of the strongest predictors of future injury: scar tissue, reduced range of motion and compensatory movement patterns all increase vulnerability.

Key Fact

The ten individual variables are: gender, age, experience, weight, fitness levels, technique/ability, nutrition/hydration, medical conditions, sleep, and previous/recurring injuries. Variables can interact — for example, a participant's weight can directly influence their fitness levels and the stress placed through their joints.

Psychological Factors

An athlete's mental state is as important as their physical condition. The specification identifies five psychological factors. Motivation affects how hard an athlete trains and whether they take appropriate rest — over-motivated athletes may overtrain, dramatically increasing overuse injury risk. Arousal refers to the athlete's level of mental and physical activation; optimal arousal improves performance, but excessive arousal leads to muscular tension, impaired decision-making and reckless movement patterns that increase injury risk. Anxiety and stress have physical consequences: elevated cortisol impairs immune function and slows tissue healing; anxiety causes muscle tension that restricts normal movement and alters gait. Confidence works both ways — a highly confident athlete may attempt skills beyond their current ability, while a low-confidence athlete may hesitate at a critical moment, exposing them to injury through poor technique or mistimed actions.

Aggression

Direct aggression — physical force directed at an opponent outside the rules of the game — is a major cause of traumatic injury, both for the aggressor and the victim. The spec distinguishes this from channelled aggression, which is the controlled use of assertiveness within the rules of the sport (e.g. a hard but fair tackle in rugby). Understanding why aggression arises helps coaches manage it. The specification identifies five reasons: level of performance (frustration when performing below expectation), retaliation (responding to a foul or provocation), pressures to win from the performer, coach or spectators, decisions of officials (perceived injustice), and performance-enhancing drugs, some of which are linked to increased aggressive behaviour.

Key Fact

Direct aggression (physical force outside the rules) is a cause of injury; channelled aggression (assertiveness within the rules) is not. The five reasons for aggression in sport are: level of performance, retaliation, pressures to win, decisions of officials, and performance-enhancing drugs.

The specification includes mental strategies as intrinsic tools for managing psychological risk. Mental rehearsal involves the athlete vividly imagining a skill being performed correctly, which reinforces correct movement patterns and reduces the chance of technique breakdown under pressure. Imagery is a broader process of creating and using mental images — including visualising a safe, controlled landing or a measured tackle — to prepare the body and mind for the demands ahead. Selective attention involves filtering out distractions such as crowd noise or crowd-induced anxiety so the athlete can focus entirely on the task, reducing the likelihood of mistimed actions. These strategies are most closely linked to the psychological benefits of a warm up, which is where they are typically applied in practice.

The spec explicitly notes that individual variables can influence one another — this is where higher-level exam answers gain marks. For example, an athlete who has poor nutrition and inadequate sleep will also have lower fitness levels and impaired tissue healing — three variables compounding each other. A previous knee injury may lead a footballer to alter their running technique, which in turn places excess stress on the opposite hip, creating a new overuse injury site. Weight can directly influence fitness levels: higher body mass demands more cardiovascular effort during the same exercise intensity, leading to earlier fatigue. In 8-mark evaluate questions, demonstrating that intrinsic factors interact rather than acting in isolation will push an answer into the Mastering band.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When asked to "compare and contrast" intrinsic factors, structure your answer around both similarities and differences. For example, both poor nutrition and lack of sleep impair tissue repair and increase fatigue — but sleep deprivation additionally impairs reaction time and coordination, which are risk factors unique to that variable. Examiners reward answers that use the precise specification vocabulary ("previous/recurring injuries", "nutrition/hydration", "technique/ability") rather than informal language. For aggression questions, always distinguish direct from channelled aggression — failing to do so typically loses a mark.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The ten individual variables (gender, age, experience, weight, fitness levels, technique/ability, nutrition/hydration, medical conditions, sleep, previous/recurring injuries) all influence injury risk and can interact with one another in ways that compound risk.
  • Psychological factors — motivation, arousal, anxiety/stress, confidence and aggression — are intrinsic risk factors because they directly affect movement quality, decision-making and behaviour during sport.
  • Mental strategies (mental rehearsal, imagery, selective attention) can reduce psychological injury risk and are closely linked to the psychological benefits of a warm up covered earlier in this unit.

lessons.title: Warm Up Routines
lessons.description: The four key components of a warm up and the physiological and psychological benefits of warming up before sport.
lessons.content_html:
Why Warm Up?

A warm up is one of the most effective single actions an athlete can take to reduce their injury risk. Both the key components and the physiological and psychological benefits are examinable — and you are expected to apply both to specific sporting scenarios. Failing to warm up is not a neutral act: it measurably increases injury risk by leaving muscles cold, joints stiff and the mind unprepared for the demands of competition.

Phase 1: Pulse Raising

The first component is pulse raising — low-to-moderate intensity continuous activity that gradually elevates heart rate, breathing rate and core body temperature. Examples include jogging around the pitch, light cycling or steady swimming. The purpose is to increase blood flow and oxygen delivery to the working muscles before the intensity of the session increases. Starting sport at a resting heart rate without a pulse raiser leaves muscles starved of the oxygen and blood flow needed for efficient contraction, dramatically increasing the risk of muscle strains. Duration is typically 5 to 10 minutes.

Phase 2: Mobility

Mobility exercises are controlled, rhythmic movements that take joints through their full range of motion — for example, arm circles, hip rotations and ankle rolls. They differ from stretching in that mobility work focuses on joint movement rather than muscle lengthening. Following the pulse raiser, mobility work reduces joint stiffness and increases the production of synovial fluid, which lubricates the joint surfaces and reduces the friction that could otherwise contribute to cartilage wear. For a basketball player, mobility work targeting the shoulder, hip and ankle joints is particularly important before the explosive jumping, pivoting and shooting demands of the game.

Key Fact

The four key components of a warm up are: (1) pulse raising, (2) mobility, (3) dynamic stretching, and (4) skill rehearsal phase. They are performed in this order — from low intensity to sport-specific activity.

Phase 3: Dynamic Stretching

Dynamic stretching involves moving through a full range of motion in a controlled way — leg swings, walking lunges, arm swings and high knees are all examples. Unlike static stretching (which is held in a fixed position and is reserved for the cool down), dynamic stretching during the warm up maintains the elevated muscle temperature achieved during pulse raising while progressively lengthening the muscles. Research shows that static stretching before sport can temporarily reduce muscle power output — this is why dynamic stretching has replaced it as the warm-up standard. Dynamic stretching directly increases muscle flexibility and pliability of ligaments and tendons, reducing the chance of strains and sprains during the main activity.

Phase 4: Skill Rehearsal Phase

The final component is the skill rehearsal phase, which bridges the general preparation of the earlier components with the specific demands of the sport. A netball player might practise passing drills, receiving and shooting; a sprinter might perform acceleration runs at 70%, 80% and then 95% of maximum effort. The skill rehearsal phase also activates the neuromuscular pathways — the communication between the brain and the muscles — so that movement patterns are crisp and reactive when the game begins. Crucially, it links directly to the psychological benefits of a warm up: practising skills in a controlled environment before competition increases confidence and concentration.

Key Fact

The six physiological benefits of a warm up are: increase in muscle temperature, increase in heart rate, increase in flexibility of muscles and joints, increase in pliability of ligaments and tendons, increase in blood flow and oxygen to muscles, and increase in the speed of muscle contraction.

Five psychological benefits are identified: the ability to heighten or control arousal levels; improved concentration and focus; increased motivation; increased confidence; and mental rehearsal. The skill rehearsal phase is the component most directly responsible for these psychological gains — practising skills successfully at the end of a warm up builds confidence and sharpens focus. Controlling arousal is particularly important: a nervous performer can use the warm up to regulate their activation level, using techniques such as controlled breathing or imagery to arrive at the optimum psychological state for performance. These benefits directly reduce injury risk by ensuring the athlete is mentally focused rather than anxious or distracted when the main activity begins.

It is important to be aware of the negative effects of not warming up. Physiologically: muscles remain cold and less elastic, dramatically increasing the risk of strains; ligaments and tendons are less pliable, raising sprain risk; heart rate and blood pressure rise too rapidly at the start of strenuous exercise, placing cardiovascular stress on the body; and the speed of muscle contraction remains low, reducing reaction time and power. Psychologically: without the skill rehearsal phase, confidence and concentration are lower; arousal may be poorly calibrated — too high (anxiety) or too low (under-arousal) — leading to reckless or sluggish movement. In exam scenarios, describing these "negative effects" is the exact mirror image of the benefits — so learning both together is highly efficient revision.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When listing physiological benefits, always begin with the phrase "increase in" — for example, "increase in muscle temperature" — because OCR mark schemes credit the exact specification wording. For a 6-mark question on warm up benefits, cover both physiological and psychological dimensions and link each benefit to a consequence: "an increase in muscle temperature leads to greater elasticity, which reduces the risk of a muscle strain." Simply listing benefits without explaining the mechanism typically scores in the Developing band only.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A complete warm up has four components performed in order: pulse raising, mobility, dynamic stretching, and skill rehearsal — each preparing the body for increasingly sport-specific demands.
  • The six physiological benefits all begin with "increase in" — muscle temperature, heart rate, flexibility, pliability of ligaments and tendons, blood flow and oxygen, and speed of muscle contraction.
  • The five psychological benefits — heightened or controlled arousal, improved concentration, increased motivation, increased confidence and mental rehearsal — reduce the risk of injury by ensuring the athlete is mentally prepared and focused before competition.

lessons.title: Cool Down Routines
lessons.description: The components of a cool down and the physiological benefits that aid recovery and reduce the risk of post-exercise.
lessons.content_html:
Why Cool Down?

The cool down is as important as the warm up, yet it is the part of a training session most commonly skipped by athletes under time pressure. The specification asks you to understand both the components of a cool down routine and the physiological benefits each component provides. Failing to cool down has measurable negative consequences — elevated post-exercise muscle soreness, blood pooling and an increased risk of Delayed Onset of Muscle Soreness (DOMS) being the most significant.

Phase 1: Pulse Lowering

The first component is pulse lowering — a gradual reduction in exercise intensity that allows the cardiovascular system to return to its resting state in a controlled manner. Examples include a slow jog transitioning to a brisk walk, or gentle cycling at low resistance. Stopping strenuous exercise abruptly causes the heart to continue pumping blood at a high rate while the muscles suddenly stop assisting venous return — this is the primary cause of blood pooling, which can cause dizziness, fainting and an unnecessarily elevated recovery heart rate. A pulse-lowering phase of 5 to 10 minutes at reducing intensity prevents this by maintaining the muscular pump action — the contraction of leg muscles that assists blood flow back to the heart — until heart rate has approached its resting value.

Key Fact

Blood pooling is the accumulation of blood in the lower limbs after exercise stops suddenly. It occurs because the muscular pump that assisted venous return ceases to operate. Pulse lowering prevents blood pooling by maintaining gentle muscular activity until heart rate returns toward its resting level.

Phase 2: Stretching

Following pulse lowering, the stretching component of a cool down uses three distinct types of stretch. Static stretches are held in a fixed position, typically for 15 to 30 seconds, and target the specific muscles used during the main activity. They are most effective during the cool down because muscles are still warm and pliable, allowing a greater range of motion. Maintenance stretches are similar to static stretches and are used to maintain the current level of flexibility — they hold the muscle at its current end range without attempting to increase it. Both static and maintenance stretches help to restore muscles to their pre-exercise length, reducing post-exercise stiffness.

Proprioceptive Neuromuscular Facilitation (PNF) is the most advanced of the three stretching methods. PNF typically involves a partner or a fixed surface: the athlete moves into a stretch, then isometrically contracts the target muscle against resistance for approximately 6 seconds, then relaxes and moves into a deeper stretch. The contraction temporarily fatigues the muscle spindle reflex that normally resists lengthening, allowing the muscle to relax further. PNF is particularly effective for athletes who need to maintain or develop flexibility as part of their sport — gymnasts and dancers, for example, frequently use PNF in cool-down routines.

Key Fact

The seven physiological benefits of a cool down are: gradually lowers heart rate; gradually lowers temperature; circulates blood and oxygen; helps prevent blood pooling; gradually reduces breathing rate; removes waste products such as lactic acid; and reduces the risk of Delayed Onset of Muscle Soreness (DOMS).

Delayed Onset of Muscle Soreness (DOMS) is the muscular pain and stiffness experienced 24 to 72 hours after unaccustomed or high-intensity exercise. It is caused primarily by microscopic damage to muscle fibres and the associated inflammatory response. Lactic acid — a waste product of anaerobic respiration — was historically blamed for DOMS, but current understanding is that it is cleared from muscles within an hour of exercise ending; the prolonged soreness of DOMS is now attributed to the inflammatory repair process in damaged fibres. A cool down helps to reduce DOMS risk by: (1) maintaining blood flow through the muscles for longer, which speeds the clearance of metabolic waste products; (2) static stretching, which may reduce the swelling associated with the inflammatory response; and (3) preventing the sudden cessation of circulation that would leave damaged fibres with less oxygen and nutrient supply during the critical early repair window.

It is important to be aware of the negative effects if no cool down is performed. Physiologically: blood may pool in the lower limbs, causing dizziness or fainting; heart rate drops too rapidly, increasing cardiovascular strain; metabolic waste products (including lactic acid) remain in the muscles for longer, contributing to increased stiffness and soreness; the risk of DOMS is significantly elevated; and muscles remain shorter than their pre-exercise length, potentially reducing flexibility over time if the pattern is repeated. There are no psychological benefits listed specifically for a cool down in the specification, but practically speaking, a rushed exit without cool down can contribute to elevated anxiety and poor readiness for the next training session. In exam answers, always mirror the specification language: "fails to gradually lower heart rate", "increases the risk of blood pooling", "delays the removal of waste products".
lessons.exam_tip_html: For questions on cool down benefits, use the word "gradually" where the specification uses it — "gradually lowers heart rate" and "gradually lowers temperature" are the exact phrases OCR awards marks for. Do not confuse cool-down stretching with warm-up stretching: the cool down uses static stretches, maintenance stretches and PNF (held positions), while the warm up uses dynamic stretching (moving). Also, remember that PNF stretching uses a contract-relax mechanism and is typically partner-assisted — giving this detail in extended answers consistently earns higher marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A cool down has two components: pulse lowering (prevents blood pooling and helps the cardiovascular system return to rest gradually) and stretching (maintenance stretches, static stretches and PNF) to restore muscle length and reduce DOMS.
  • The seven physiological benefits of a cool down are: gradually lowering heart rate, lowering temperature, circulating blood and oxygen, preventing blood pooling, gradually reducing breathing rate, removing waste products such as lactic acid, and reducing the risk of DOMS.
  • PNF stretching uses a contract-relax mechanism to achieve a greater range of motion than static stretching alone and is the most advanced stretching technique covered in this unit.

lessons.title: Types and Causes of Sports Injuries
lessons.description: Acute and chronic sports injuries — their causes, symptoms and whether they affect soft or hard tissue.
lessons.content_html:
Acute vs Chronic Injuries

Sports injuries fall into two fundamental categories. Acute injuries are caused by a single sudden traumatic event — a collision, a fall, a missed landing. They have an immediate onset, with pain typically felt instantly. Chronic injuries, by contrast, develop gradually through repetitive movement and overuse; the athlete may notice a dull ache that worsens over weeks or months rather than a sharp pain at a defined moment. Distinguishing these two categories is a foundation of this unit, and the distinction comes up in both short-answer and extended-response exam questions.

Soft Tissue vs Hard Tissue Injuries

Injuries are also classified by which type of body tissue is damaged. Soft-tissue injuries involve muscles, tendons, ligaments, cartilage or skin. Hard-tissue injuries involve bone, including fractures and dislocations. This classification helps to determine treatment: hard-tissue injuries typically require imaging (X-ray) and immobilisation, while soft-tissue injuries may be managed with PRICE therapy and physiotherapy.

Acute Soft-Tissue Injuries: Strains and Sprains

A strain is a tear or overstretching of a muscle or tendon. Strains occur when a muscle is asked to generate force it cannot sustain — for example, a sprinter pulling their hamstring during maximum acceleration, or a weightlifter straining their lower back. Strains are soft-tissue injuries. A sprain, by contrast, is a tear of a ligament — the fibrous tissue that connects bone to bone and stabilises joints. Sprains most commonly affect the ankle, knee and wrist. The most clinically significant ligament in sport is the Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL), located in the knee: ACL injuries typically occur during sudden direction changes, landing from a jump, or deceleration — making them particularly common in football, netball and basketball. Both strains and sprains are acute soft-tissue injuries.

Key Fact

A strain is a torn or overstretched muscle or tendon (soft tissue). A sprain is a torn ligament (soft tissue). The Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) in the knee is the most clinically important ligament in sport science and is commonly injured through sudden twisting or deceleration movements.

Acute Skin Damage: Abrasions, Contusions and Blisters

Skin damage encompasses four types in the specification. Abrasions (grazes) occur when the skin surface is scraped against a hard surface — a rugby player sliding on an artificial pitch or a cyclist falling on a road. Cuts and lacerations involve a break in the skin caused by sharp contact with an implement, a surface or an opponent. Contusions (bruises) result from a direct blow that damages blood vessels beneath the skin without breaking the surface — the bleeding is internal, causing the characteristic discolouration. Blisters are fluid-filled pockets beneath the skin caused by repetitive friction — a rower's hands, a runner's heels and a tennis player's fingers are all common sites. All of these are soft-tissue injuries. They vary in severity: lacerations and contusions can occasionally be serious (a deep laceration may require suturing; a contusion on the head may mask a more serious injury), while abrasions and blisters are typically minor but can become infected if poorly managed.

Acute Hard-Tissue Injuries: Fractures and Dislocations

A fracture is a break in a bone. The specification distinguishes two types. An open (compound) fracture is where the broken bone penetrates through the skin — highly visible, carries a serious infection risk and always requires emergency medical attention. A closed (simple) fracture is where the bone breaks internally without breaking the skin, identified by pain, swelling, deformity and loss of function. A dislocation occurs when the bones of a joint are forced out of their normal anatomical alignment — the shoulder (glenohumeral joint) and fingers are the most commonly dislocated joints in sport. Dislocations are hard-tissue injuries. They typically cause immediate severe pain, a visible deformity and complete loss of normal joint function. Fractures and dislocations must not be manipulated in the field without medical expertise — a suspected fracture or dislocation should be immobilised and the athlete referred immediately to emergency services.

Key Fact

Hard-tissue injuries are limited to fractures (open and closed), stress fractures and dislocations. Every other named injury in the specification — strains, sprains, abrasions, contusions, blisters, concussion, tendonitis, epicondylitis and shin splints — is a soft-tissue injury.

Concussion is a traumatic brain injury caused by a blow or jolt to the head that temporarily disrupts normal brain function. Symptoms include headache, confusion, dizziness, nausea, memory problems and sensitivity to light. The specification requires you to know the possible link between repeated head injuries and the onset of dementia and Alzheimer's disease. This link has become a major safeguarding concern in contact sports, particularly rugby union and American football. Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy (CTE) — a degenerative brain condition found post-mortem in former contact sport athletes — is now associated with a history of repeated concussive and sub-concussive blows. As a result, national governing bodies (NGBs) have introduced strict return-to-play protocols: no athlete with suspected concussion should return to play in the same session. Concussion is a soft-tissue injury (brain tissue, not bone).

Chronic injuries develop gradually from repetitive overuse. Tendonitis is inflammation of a tendon caused by repetitive stress. The three named sites are: Achilles tendonitis (posterior heel — common in runners and jumpers); rotator cuff tendonitis (shoulder — common in swimmers, throwers and racket sport players); and patellar tendonitis (knee — common in basketball players and high jumpers, nicknamed "jumper's knee"). Epicondylitis is inflammation of the epicondyle of the humerus (the bony projection at the elbow). Lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow) causes pain on the outside of the elbow through overuse of the wrist extensor muscles — common in racket sports and repetitive manual tasks. Medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow) causes pain on the inside of the elbow through overuse of the wrist flexors — common in golf, throwing sports and rock climbing. Shin splints (medial tibial stress syndrome) cause pain along the inner shin, typically in runners who rapidly increase their training mileage, run on hard surfaces or have poor footwear. Stress fractures are tiny cracks in bone from repetitive loading — unlike other chronic injuries, they are hard-tissue injuries. All tendonitis, epicondylitis and shin splints are soft-tissue injuries.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When answering "compare and contrast" questions on acute vs chronic injuries, structure your response around three dimensions: onset (sudden vs gradual), cause (single traumatic event vs repetitive overuse) and typical tissue affected (both can be soft tissue, but only acute injuries include hard-tissue fractures and dislocations as common presentations). For questions on specific injuries, always state whether the injured structure is soft tissue or hard tissue — this earns a mark in questions that ask you to "classify" or "describe" the injury type. Never confuse strain (muscle/tendon) with sprain (ligament).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Acute injuries result from a single sudden traumatic event (fractures, dislocations, strains, sprains, abrasions, contusions, concussion) while chronic injuries develop gradually through repetitive overuse (tendonitis, epicondylitis, shin splints, stress fractures).
  • Hard-tissue injuries are limited to fractures (open and closed), stress fractures and dislocations; all other named injuries — including strains, sprains, tendonitis and concussion — are soft-tissue injuries.
  • A strain is a torn muscle or tendon; a sprain is a torn ligament — confusing these two is one of the most common errors in exam answers and consistently loses marks.

A 16-year-old basketball player has been experiencing a dull ache in the front of her knee for six weeks. It worsens during and after training sessions.

Two plausible named injuries discussed: patellar tendonitis (inflammation of the patellar tendon below the kneecap — common in jumping sports, nicknamed "jumper's knee") and a stress fracture (tiny crack in the patellar or tibial bone from repetitive loading — hard tissue). The distinction between soft-tissue (patellar tendonitis) and hard-tissue (stress fracture) injuries is noted. Both candidates discussed with their causes applied to the scenario.
Secure (3-4 marks): Correctly identifies chronic injury, names two candidates with brief explanation and some reference to basketball.

practice_questions.text:
A national rugby union governing body is developing a new player welfare policy following concerns about the long-term effects of concussion in the sport.

Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points largely one-sided or without a clear judgement.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points about concussion with little development and no evaluation. [8 marks]

lessons.title: Responding to Sports Injuries: First Aid (SALTAPS & PRICE)
lessons.description: How to assess an injured performer using SALTAPS and manage soft-tissue injuries with PRICE and DRABC.
lessons.content_html:
Why First Aid Matters in Sport

Every sports session carries some risk of injury. When something goes wrong, a coach, referee or first aider must act quickly and correctly. Knowing the right assessment and treatment protocols can prevent a minor injury from becoming a serious one, and could even save a life. Two of the most important tools in sport first aid are the SALTAPS protocol and the PRICE therapy framework.

SALTAPS: The On-Field Assessment

SALTAPS is a seven-step routine for assessing an injured performer on the pitch or court. It helps the first responder gather information systematically before deciding whether the athlete can continue, needs to be removed, or requires emergency help. The steps are as follows.

See — observe the incident as it happens or arrive on the scene and look for obvious signs of injury such as unusual posture, swelling or deformity. Ask — question the performer about what happened, where it hurts and what the pain feels like; this gives subjective information that cannot be seen. Look — carry out a visual inspection of the injured area, comparing it to the uninjured side; look for swelling, bruising, redness or deformity. Touch — with the performer’s permission, gently palpate (feel) the area to identify specific points of tenderness or crepitus (a grinding sensation that may indicate a fracture).

Active movement — ask the performer to move the injured part themselves (without assistance) through their pain-free range; this tests whether the muscles and tendons are working. Passive movement — the first aider gently moves the injured joint while the performer’s muscles remain relaxed; this tests the integrity of ligaments and joint structures. Strength testing — the performer resists gentle pressure applied by the first aider; if this is pain-free and strength is maintained, return to play may be considered. If any step reveals a significant problem, the performer should be removed and further assessment arranged.

Key Fact

SALTAPS stands for See, Ask, Look, Touch, Active movement, Passive movement, Strength testing. It is the standard on-field assessment routine used to decide whether an injured performer can continue or must be removed from play.

DRABC: Emergency First Aid

If a performer is unconscious or you suspect a life-threatening emergency, SALTAPS is set aside and the DRABC protocol takes over. Danger — ensure the scene is safe for you, the performer and bystanders before approaching. Response — check for consciousness by calling the performer’s name and tapping their shoulders firmly. Airway — if unresponsive, open the airway by tilting the head back and lifting the chin. Breathing — look, listen and feel for normal breathing for up to 10 seconds. Circulation — if the performer is not breathing normally, call emergency services immediately and begin CPR at 30 chest compressions to 2 rescue breaths.

If a performer is unconscious but breathing normally and has no life-threatening conditions, place them in the recovery position: roll them onto their side, support the head and tilt it back slightly to keep the airway clear, and ensure the top knee is bent to prevent rolling forward. Monitor their breathing continuously until emergency services arrive.

SALTAPS is for alert, conscious performers who have sustained a musculoskeletal injury such as a sprain or strain. The moment a performer is unresponsive, unconscious, not breathing normally, or you suspect cardiac arrest, DRABC must be applied immediately. Never delay DRABC to complete a SALTAPS assessment. The priority order in any emergency is always: safety first, then airway, then circulation. Calling 999 (or 112) early is critical — a defibrillator should be retrieved while CPR begins.

PRICE Therapy: Immediate Soft-Tissue Management

Once a conscious performer with a soft-tissue injury (sprain, strain or contusion) has been assessed and removed from play, PRICE therapy guides the immediate treatment. Applied within the first 24–72 hours, it limits swelling, reduces pain and creates the best conditions for healing.

Protection — protect the injury from further damage, for example by using a splint, sling or by simply stopping the performer from weight-bearing. Rest — stop physical activity to prevent aggravation; this does not mean total bed rest but avoidance of the activity that caused the injury. Ice — apply a cold pack or ice wrapped in a damp cloth for 15–20 minutes every two hours; never apply ice directly to skin as this risks an ice burn. Compression — apply a firm (but not tight) bandage to reduce swelling and provide support. Elevation — raise the injured limb above the level of the heart to reduce blood pooling and oedema.

Key Fact

PRICE stands for Protection, Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation. Each step targets a different aspect of the inflammatory response: protection prevents further damage, ice and compression reduce swelling, and elevation drains excess fluid away from the injury site.

X-rays and Specialist Assessment

When a fracture is suspected following the SALTAPS assessment — for example, if there is point tenderness over bone, obvious deformity or the performer cannot bear weight — the performer must be referred for an X-ray. X-rays detect whether bones are broken and whether a fracture is open or closed. You do not need to understand the technical process of how X-rays work, but you must know that they are the primary imaging tool used to diagnose skeletal injury in sport.

A very common error both in practice and in exam answers is stating that ice should be applied directly to the skin. This causes an ice burn (frostbite injury to the superficial tissues) and is incorrect. Ice must always be wrapped in a damp cloth or placed in an ice bag with a cloth barrier. Similarly, do not state that compression should be applied as tightly as possible — a bandage that is too tight can restrict circulation. If a performer’s fingers or toes become pale, cold or numb after bandaging, the bandage is too tight and must be loosened immediately.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In exam questions about SALTAPS, you will often be given a scenario describing what a first aider does and asked to name the step. Learn each letter’s meaning precisely — confusing ‘Active’ (performer moves themselves) with ‘Passive’ (first aider moves the limb) is a very common error. For PRICE questions, always state what each step achieves, not just what it involves: for example, elevation ‘reduces swelling by draining excess fluid away from the injured site’ earns more marks than simply ‘raise the leg’.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • SALTAPS (See, Ask, Look, Touch, Active, Passive, Strength) is the systematic on-field assessment used to decide whether an injured performer can continue; if a performer is unconscious or not breathing, switch immediately to DRABC and call 999.
  • PRICE therapy (Protection, Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation) is the first-line treatment for soft-tissue injuries applied within the first 24–72 hours; ice must never be applied directly to skin.
  • An unconscious performer who is breathing should be placed in the recovery position to keep the airway clear; X-rays are used when a fracture is suspected following field assessment.

lessons.title: Rehabilitation & Reducing the Risk of Injury
lessons.description: Treatments and therapies used in rehabilitation, plus key strategies for reducing the risk of sports injuries.
lessons.content_html:
From Treatment to Full Recovery

Once immediate first aid has been given, the focus shifts to rehabilitation. Effective rehabilitation is not simply resting until the pain fades — it is a structured programme of treatments and exercises that progressively restore strength, range of movement and confidence. Getting rehabilitation right determines how quickly, and how safely, an athlete returns to their sport.

Treatments and Therapies in Rehabilitation

A range of treatments can be used at different stages of the rehabilitation process. Massage increases blood flow to the injured tissue, reduces muscle tension and can break down scar tissue during later stages of recovery. Ultrasound therapy uses sound waves to promote tissue healing and reduce inflammation; it is particularly useful for deep soft-tissue injuries such as ligament sprains.

Electrotherapy uses electrical stimulation (such as TENS) to reduce pain and stimulate muscle contractions in weakened muscles. Hydrotherapy involves exercising in water, where buoyancy reduces the load on injured joints, allowing the performer to rebuild strength and range of movement with less pain. Cryotherapy — the therapeutic use of cold — reduces pain, swelling and inflammation; it may be applied as ice packs, ice baths or localised cold-air devices. Contrast therapy alternates between cold and warm water immersion to stimulate blood flow, reduce swelling and speed tissue recovery.

Painkillers such as ibuprofen (an anti-inflammatory) can reduce pain and swelling, allowing the performer to engage in therapeutic exercises. However, they mask pain signals, so return to activity must be managed carefully. Support in the form of kinesiology taping, neoprene sleeves or bandaging provides stability to healing structures and proprioceptive feedback. Immobilisation via a cast, splint or sling is used when a bone or severely injured joint must be held still to heal correctly — for example, following a fracture or dislocation.

Key Fact

The main rehabilitation treatments are: massage, ultrasound, electrotherapy, hydrotherapy, cryotherapy, contrast therapy, painkillers (e.g. ibuprofen), kinesiology taping / neoprene / bandaging, and immobilisation (cast / splint / sling). Each is used at different stages and for different injury types.

Psychological Effects of Injury

Injury does not only affect the body. The psychological impact of being unable to train or compete can be significant. Athletes may experience frustration, anxiety, low mood, reduced confidence and fear of re-injury. During long-term rehabilitation, motivation can drop as progress slows. Mental strategies such as mental rehearsal (imagining performing skills correctly), imagery, and goal-setting are used by sports psychologists and physiotherapists to maintain an athlete's psychological wellbeing and confidence throughout the recovery process.

Stretching is not just a cool-down component — it is also a key rehabilitation tool. Maintenance stretches and static stretches applied during rehabilitation restore the normal length of healing muscle fibres, prevent scar tissue contracture and gradually improve range of movement at the injured joint. Proprioceptive Neuromuscular Facilitation (PNF) stretching — where the muscle is contracted and then stretched — is particularly effective in the later stages of rehabilitation to regain full flexibility. This is why warm-up and cool-down stretching techniques are directly linked to injury treatment.

Reducing the Risk of Injury

Prevention is always better than cure. Several strategies are used before and during sporting participation to reduce the likelihood and severity of injury. Safety checks and risk assessments involve systematically identifying hazards in the environment (e.g. wet playing surfaces, damaged equipment) and assessing the level of risk, then implementing control measures to remove or reduce those hazards. Risk assessments also consider the characteristics of the group — age, experience, medical conditions and group size all affect the level of supervision and precautions needed.

Medical screening identifies pre-existing conditions that could increase injury risk. Athletes may complete health questionnaires, undergo physical examinations or electrocardiograms (ECGs) before contact sport. National Governing Body (NGB) policies set mandatory safety standards — for example, World Rugby's protocols on concussion management, or the FA's rules on heading in youth football — that all affiliated clubs must follow.

Emergency Action Plans (EAPs) are written documents that specify in advance: which personnel are responsible for emergency response (emergency personnel), how communication to emergency services will be made (emergency communication), and which equipment such as defibrillators, first aid kits and stretchers is available and where (emergency equipment). An EAP ensures that everyone knows their role the moment an emergency occurs, reducing response time and potential harm.

Key Fact

An Emergency Action Plan (EAP) has three components: emergency personnel (who responds), emergency communication (how to contact services) and emergency equipment (what is available and where). Having an EAP in place means no time is wasted deciding what to do when an emergency occurs.

Students often confuse cryotherapy (cold only) with contrast therapy (alternating cold and warm). Cryotherapy uses cold alone — ice packs, ice baths or cold-air devices — to reduce acute inflammation and pain. Contrast therapy alternates between cold and warm immersion (for example, 1 minute cold water, 3 minutes warm water, repeated) to stimulate blood flow changes that aid recovery. They are different treatments used at different points in rehabilitation. In an exam, if asked to describe cryotherapy, do not mention warm water.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For questions about rehabilitation treatments, always name the treatment precisely and state the benefit it provides. Saying 'massage helps the injury' earns no marks. Saying 'massage increases blood flow to the injured tissue, which delivers oxygen and nutrients needed for cell repair' earns full marks. For EAP questions, remember all three components: personnel, communication and equipment — missing one will cost you a mark.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Rehabilitation uses a range of named treatments — including massage, ultrasound, hydrotherapy, cryotherapy, contrast therapy, electrotherapy, painkillers, taping and immobilisation — applied at different stages and for different injury types to restore function safely.
  • Injury also has significant psychological effects including anxiety, loss of confidence and fear of re-injury; mental strategies such as imagery and mental rehearsal support psychological recovery alongside physical treatment.
  • The risk of injury is reduced through safety checks and risk assessments, medical screening, NGB policies, and Emergency Action Plans (EAPs) covering personnel, communication and equipment.

lessons.title: Common Medical Conditions: Asthma & Diabetes
lessons.description: Causes, symptoms and management of asthma and diabetes (Type 1, Type 2, hypoglycaemia, hyperglycaemia) in sport.
lessons.content_html:
Medical Conditions in Sport

Many sports performers live with long-term medical conditions. Asthma and diabetes are two of the most common conditions encountered in sport. Understanding their causes, symptoms and management is essential for coaches, teachers and performers so that participation can continue safely and emergencies can be handled correctly.

Asthma: Causes and Triggers

Asthma is a chronic respiratory condition in which the airways become inflamed, narrow and produce excess mucus, making breathing difficult. The exact cause of asthma is not fully understood, but two key triggers are especially relevant in sport. Environmental triggers include cold air, air pollution, pollen, dust, pet dander and cigarette smoke — all of which can inflame the airways. Exercise is a particularly important trigger: during vigorous physical activity, increased ventilation draws cold, dry air deep into the airways, which can provoke an asthma attack — sometimes called exercise-induced bronchoconstriction.

Asthma: Symptoms and Treatment

The four key symptoms of asthma are: coughing (often worse at night or after exercise), wheezing (a whistling or rattling sound on breathing out), shortness of breath (difficulty getting enough air, particularly during exertion) and tightness in the chest (a squeezing feeling that can feel like pressure). During an asthma attack all four symptoms may occur together and can escalate rapidly.

Treatment in a sporting context has two elements: reassurance — remaining calm, helping the performer sit upright in a position that opens the chest, and reassuring them reduces anxiety, which otherwise worsens the attack; and inhalers or nebulisers — a reliever inhaler (usually blue) delivers bronchodilator medication (typically salbutamol) that relaxes the airway muscles and opens the airways within minutes. A nebuliser delivers the same medication as a fine mist for more severe cases. If a performer's reliever inhaler does not work after 10 puffs, or if they become very distressed or their lips turn blue, call 999 immediately.

Key Fact

The four symptoms of asthma are coughing, wheezing, shortness of breath and tightness in the chest. Treatment involves reassurance and a reliever inhaler (or nebuliser). If the inhaler fails after 10 puffs, call 999 immediately.

Diabetes: Type 1 and Type 2

Diabetes is a condition in which the body cannot regulate insulin correctly, leading to abnormal blood sugar levels. There are two main types. Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition typically diagnosed in childhood or young adulthood — the body's immune system destroys the insulin-producing cells in the pancreas, so the body produces no insulin at all and the person is entirely dependent on insulin injections or a pump. Type 2 diabetes is much more common and is strongly linked to lifestyle factors such as a poor diet and physical inactivity; the body either does not produce enough insulin or the cells become resistant to it. Type 2 is more commonly diagnosed in adults, though increasing numbers of young people are affected.

Diabetes: Symptoms and Treatment

Common symptoms of both Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes include: increased thirst (the body tries to dilute excess blood sugar by drawing water from cells), urinating more often (kidneys filter excess glucose through urine), extreme tiredness (cells cannot access glucose for energy), unexplained weight loss and cuts or wounds that take a long time to heal (high blood sugar impairs immune function and circulation). These symptoms are shared across both types, though Type 1 tends to develop more rapidly.

Treatment differs by type: Type 1 requires daily insulin injections or an insulin pump, as well as careful diet management. Type 2 is often managed initially through lifestyle changes — including increased physical activity and a healthier diet — with medication or insulin added if lifestyle changes are insufficient. Both types require regular blood sugar monitoring, especially around exercise, as physical activity significantly affects blood glucose levels.

Key Fact

Type 1 diabetes: the body cannot produce insulin (autoimmune). Type 2 diabetes: the body does not produce enough insulin or insulin does not work properly (lifestyle-linked). Both types share the same five common symptoms.

Blood Sugar Levels: Hypos and Hyperglycaemia

Blood sugar levels in a diabetic performer can fall dangerously low or rise dangerously high, both of which are medical emergencies. Hypoglycaemia (a 'hypo') occurs when blood sugar falls too low — often triggered by exercise, missed meals or too much insulin. Symptoms include shakiness, sweating, dizziness, confusion, pallor and weakness. Treatment is rapid ingestion of fast-acting glucose (e.g. glucose tablets, a sugary drink or orange juice). Exercise significantly increases the risk of a hypo in Type 1 diabetics, so blood sugar should be checked before, during and after activity. Hyperglycaemia (high blood sugar) develops more slowly — caused by too little insulin, too many carbohydrates or illness — and symptoms include increased thirst, frequent urination and fatigue. Severe hyperglycaemia requires medical attention.

A performer with asthma should always have their reliever inhaler immediately accessible during sport — not locked away in a bag or locker. A thorough warm-up is especially important because it gradually raises ventilation rather than shocking the airways with sudden intense effort. In cold weather, wearing a scarf or sports buff over the mouth and nose warms and humidifies the inhaled air, reducing the exercise-induced trigger. Coaches should know which performers have asthma, where their inhalers are kept, and the action to take if an attack occurs.

A Type 1 diabetic performer should check blood glucose before exercise and have fast-acting carbohydrates (e.g. glucose tablets or a sports drink) immediately to hand during activity. If blood sugar is low before training, a carbohydrate snack should be eaten and glucose rechecked before starting. Exercise generally lowers blood sugar, so insulin doses may need adjusting on training days — this should always be done in consultation with a medical professional. Coaches should know the signs of a hypo and have access to glucose sources at the venue.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When answering questions about diabetes, be precise about the cause: Type 1 is 'the body cannot produce insulin' and Type 2 is 'the body does not produce enough insulin or the insulin does not work properly'. Do not say Type 2 is simply 'diet-related' — this is too vague. For hypoglycaemia questions, state the treatment as 'fast-acting glucose / a sugary drink', not just 'eat something'. Accuracy on medical conditions is directly linked to marks.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Asthma symptoms are coughing, wheezing, shortness of breath and chest tightness; treatment is reassurance plus a reliever inhaler, with 999 called if the inhaler fails after 10 puffs.
  • Type 1 diabetes means the body cannot produce insulin; Type 2 means it does not produce enough or insulin does not work properly; both share symptoms of increased thirst, frequent urination, extreme tiredness, weight loss and slow-healing cuts.
  • Hypoglycaemia (low blood sugar) is treated with fast-acting glucose and is a particular risk during exercise; hyperglycaemia (high blood sugar) develops more slowly and requires medical attention if severe.

Specific measures are then evaluated (inhaler on site, blood sugar checks, warm-up protocols, emergency plans) and a judgement reached — e.g. that full inclusion is the right approach when appropriate management protocols are in place, but blanket inclusion without individual risk assessment is not responsible.

lessons.title: Common Medical Conditions: Epilepsy & Sudden Cardiac Arrest
lessons.description: Causes, symptoms and treatment of epilepsy and sudden cardiac arrest, including AED use, CPR and cardiac arrest vs.
lessons.content_html:
Two Serious Conditions in Sport

Epilepsy and sudden cardiac arrest (SCA) are two of the most serious medical conditions a coach or sports practitioner may encounter. Both can be life-threatening in a sporting context. Understanding the causes, recognising the symptoms and knowing the correct response can make the difference between life and death. This lesson covers both conditions in the depth required by the specification.

Epilepsy: Overview and Causes

Epilepsy is a neurological condition in which abnormal bursts of electrical activity in the brain cause recurrent seizures. Not all seizures are the dramatic convulsions often associated with epilepsy — they range from brief lapses in consciousness to full body shaking. Three key triggers are listed in the specification: severe head injuries (which can damage brain tissue and disrupt normal electrical patterns), anxiety or stress (psychological states that can lower the seizure threshold in susceptible individuals) and tiredness or lack of sleep (fatigue reduces the brain's resilience to abnormal electrical activity). In sport, these triggers are all plausible — contact sport carries head injury risk, competition brings stress, and overtrained athletes may be sleep-deprived.

Epilepsy: Symptoms of Seizures

Seizure symptoms affect different parts of the body. In the eyes, a performer may stare blankly or show flickering/fluttering of the eyelids — this may look like a brief lapse of attention or a temporary absence. In the mouth, symptoms include biting the tongue, making random involuntary noises or vocalisation, or producing excessive saliva. In the limbs, seizures may cause stiffness (tonic phase) followed by rhythmic jerking movements of the arms and legs (clonic phase), or sudden loss of muscle tone causing the performer to collapse to the ground.

Key Fact

Epilepsy seizure symptoms affect: eyes (staring blankly, fluttering), mouth (biting tongue, random noises) and limbs (stiffness and jerking movements). The three main triggers in sport are severe head injuries, anxiety/stress and tiredness/lack of sleep.

Epilepsy: Treatment

The two main treatments for epilepsy are anti-epileptic drugs (AEDs) — medication taken regularly to reduce the frequency and severity of seizures by stabilising the brain's electrical activity — and the ketogenic diet, a high-fat, very low-carbohydrate diet that has been shown to reduce seizure frequency in some patients, particularly children, when medication is not fully effective. In a sporting context, if a performer has a seizure, the immediate response is to protect them from injury (move hard objects away, cushion the head), do not restrain them, place them in the recovery position once convulsions stop, stay with them and call 999 if the seizure lasts more than 5 minutes or they do not regain consciousness.

A performer with epilepsy should inform their coach and ensure the coaching team know their seizure plan. Sports that involve heights, open water or fast-moving equipment carry additional risk and may require adapted supervision or individual risk assessments. During a seizure, never put anything in the performer's mouth (contrary to myth, swallowing the tongue is not possible). Head protection and the avoidance of severe head trauma are important preventive measures given the link between head injury and seizure triggers.

Sudden Cardiac Arrest: Overview and Causes

Sudden cardiac arrest (SCA) occurs when the heart's electrical system malfunctions, causing it to stop pumping blood. Without immediate treatment, brain damage begins within 4–6 minutes and death within 10 minutes. Three causes are listed in the specification: underlying genetic heart conditions — such as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), an inherited thickening of the heart muscle that is the most common cause of SCA in young athletes; intense physical activity — which can trigger SCA in those with undetected heart conditions by placing extreme demand on an already abnormal heart; and sudden trauma — a severe blow to the chest at a specific moment in the cardiac cycle (called commotio cordis) can trigger ventricular fibrillation.

SCA vs Heart Attack: A Critical Distinction

The specification requires you to know the difference between cardiac arrest and a heart attack. A heart attack (myocardial infarction) is caused by a blockage in a coronary artery — the heart muscle is starved of blood but continues to beat. The performer is typically conscious, may experience crushing chest pain, breathlessness and pain radiating to the arm or jaw, and can often speak. A sudden cardiac arrest is an electrical failure — the heart stops beating effectively. The performer is unconscious and not breathing normally. Both are emergencies requiring 999, but SCA additionally requires immediate CPR and defibrillation to have any chance of survival.

Key Fact

Sudden cardiac arrest: the heart stops beating (unconscious, not breathing normally) — requires CPR and a defibrillator immediately. Heart attack: a blocked coronary artery starves heart muscle of blood but the heart keeps beating — the performer is conscious. Both require 999 but only SCA requires CPR and defibrillation.

SCA Treatment: CPR and Defibrillation

The symptoms of SCA are: unconsciousness (sudden collapse with no response) and breathing difficulties (agonal breathing — irregular gasping — or complete absence of breathing). Treatment follows the DRABC protocol. Once SCA is suspected, call 999 immediately and begin CPR — 30 chest compressions to 2 rescue breaths, at a rate of 100–120 compressions per minute, pushing down 5–6 cm on the centre of the chest. A defibrillator (AED) should be retrieved and used as soon as possible — the AED analyses the heart rhythm and delivers a controlled electric shock if ventricular fibrillation is detected, which can restore a normal rhythm. Every minute without defibrillation reduces survival chances by approximately 10%. Lifestyle changes — including maintaining a healthy weight, not smoking, and regular cardiovascular exercise — reduce the long-term risk of cardiac events.

In the epilepsy section, the specification abbreviates anti-epileptic drugs as 'AEDs'. In the cardiac arrest section, 'AED' means Automated External Defibrillator. These are two completely different things. In an exam, always write the full term first — 'anti-epileptic drugs (AEDs)' or 'Automated External Defibrillator (AED)' — and then use the abbreviation, so the examiner can be certain which you mean. Confusing the two would result in a medically incorrect answer and lost marks.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For epilepsy questions, use the specification's exact body-area framework for symptoms: eyes, mouth, limbs — then give one example for each. For SCA questions, be precise about the treatment sequence: call 999, begin CPR (30:2), retrieve and use AED. Do not say 'give CPR' without specifying the compression-to-breath ratio. Always state the key distinction: in cardiac arrest the performer is unconscious and not breathing; in a heart attack they are conscious. This distinction is worth at least 1 mark in any comparison question.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Epilepsy seizures are triggered by severe head injuries, anxiety/stress and tiredness; symptoms affect the eyes (staring, fluttering), mouth (biting tongue, random noises) and limbs (stiffness and jerking); treatment is anti-epileptic drugs or a ketogenic diet.
  • Sudden cardiac arrest occurs when the heart stops beating, causing unconsciousness and abnormal or absent breathing; it must be distinguished from a heart attack, where the heart still beats and the performer remains conscious.
  • Treatment for SCA requires immediate 999 call, CPR (30 chest compressions to 2 rescue breaths) and an AED (Automated External Defibrillator) as soon as possible; every minute without defibrillation reduces survival odds by approximately 10%.

lessons.title: Managing Medical Conditions: Hypothermia, Heat Exhaustion & Dehydration
lessons.description: Causes, symptoms and treatment of hypothermia, heat exhaustion and dehydration, plus managing conditions in a.
lessons.content_html:
Environmental and Fluid-Related Conditions in Sport

Alongside the conditions covered in earlier lessons, sports performers are also at risk from conditions caused by the external environment and inadequate hydration. Hypothermia, heat exhaustion and dehydration are all examinable in this unit. Each is directly linked to the extrinsic factors studied earlier, particularly weather and temperature conditions.

Hypothermia: Causes and Symptoms

Hypothermia occurs when the body's core temperature drops below 35 degrees Celsius. In sport, the two key causes are: the body losing heat faster than it can produce it in cold conditions (body temperature drops below 35°C) and prolonged exposure to cold or wet conditions — for example, a cross-country runner in rain and wind, an open-water swimmer or a cyclist descending a mountain. Inadequate clothing significantly increases this risk.

The five symptoms of hypothermia listed in the specification are: shivering (the body's automatic attempt to generate heat through muscle activity), blue lips or skin (cyanosis — reduced blood flow to the periphery as the body prioritises core organs), slurred speech (cold affects neuromuscular coordination), tiredness or confusion (the brain functions less effectively as core temperature falls) and slow breathing (respiratory rate drops as metabolism slows in the cold).

Hypothermia: Treatment

Treatment for hypothermia involves gently warming the performer. The two specification treatments are: remove wet clothing and wrap in blankets, covering the head (wet clothing conducts heat away from the body rapidly, so removal and insulation are the first priority — covering the head is important because significant heat loss occurs through the scalp) and give a warm, sugary, non-alcoholic drink (warm fluids raise core temperature from the inside; sugar provides a rapid energy source; alcohol must be avoided as it causes blood vessels near the skin to dilate, actually increasing heat loss).

Key Fact

Hypothermia must NOT be treated with a hot bath, hot water bottle, or by rubbing the body parts — these cause rapid vasodilation that can send cold blood from the periphery to the core, causing cardiac complications. Warming must be gradual and gentle.

Heat Exhaustion: Causes and Symptoms

Heat exhaustion occurs when the body overheats, typically with a temperature of 38 degrees Celsius or above. Three causes are listed: body temperature reaching 38°C or above (the body's thermoregulatory mechanisms begin to fail), strenuous physical activity (generating high levels of internal heat that the body cannot dissipate fast enough) and not enough water intake (without adequate fluid, sweating — the primary cooling mechanism — is impaired). Hot, humid environments make heat exhaustion more likely because high humidity prevents sweat from evaporating effectively.

The five symptoms of heat exhaustion are: excessive sweating (the body's cooling attempt, which causes significant fluid loss), headache or dizziness (dehydration and reduced blood pressure to the brain), being very thirsty (the body signals its fluid deficit), feeling or being sick (nausea and vomiting caused by dehydration and heat stress on the gastrointestinal system) and rapid pulse and/or rapid breathing (the cardiovascular system working harder to circulate blood and transfer heat to the skin).

Heat Exhaustion: Treatment

Treatment for heat exhaustion is straightforward and must be applied quickly before the condition deteriorates into heatstroke (a life-threatening emergency). The two specification treatments are: move the performer to a cool place and cool their skin — for example, move them into the shade or an air-conditioned area, loosen clothing, apply cool damp cloths to the skin or use a fan — and get them to drink plenty of water to replace the fluid lost through sweating. If the performer does not improve within 30 minutes or becomes confused or loses consciousness, call 999.

Key Fact

Hypothermia: core body temperature below 35°C. Heat exhaustion: body temperature of 38°C or above. These are the threshold temperatures specified by the specification and must be learned precisely.

Dehydration: Causes, Symptoms and Treatment

Dehydration is caused by loss of bodily fluids — primarily through sweating during exercise — that are not adequately replaced. In sport, dehydration impairs thermoregulation, reduces blood volume, slows reaction times and decreases strength and aerobic capacity. There is a direct link between dehydration and both diabetes — because high blood sugar causes the kidneys to excrete more water — and heat exhaustion, since dehydration prevents effective sweating.

The four symptoms of dehydration are: feeling thirsty (thirst is actually a late sign — by the time you feel thirsty, performance is already impaired), fatigue (reduced blood volume means less oxygen delivered to muscles), dark yellow urine and infrequent urination (the kidneys conserve water by concentrating urine — pale urine indicates good hydration; dark urine indicates dehydration) and dry mouth or lips (reduced saliva production as the body conserves fluid). Treatment is simple: drink plenty of water as the first step, with rehydration sachets (oral rehydration salts) used in cases of significant fluid and electrolyte loss to restore the correct balance of water and minerals.

The best approach to dehydration in sport is prevention. Performers should hydrate well before training, drink regularly during activity (approximately 150–250 ml every 15–20 minutes in moderate conditions, more in heat), and continue rehydrating after training. Coaches should build regular drink breaks into sessions and ensure water is always available at training venues. Monitoring urine colour is a practical and reliable way for performers to self-assess hydration status. Diabetic performers must be especially vigilant as high blood sugar can cause increased urination (polyuria), accelerating dehydration.

The specification explicitly links weather and temperature conditions to medical risk. Cold, wet weather increases hypothermia risk — appropriate clothing and a warm-up that raises core temperature both mitigate this. Hot, humid conditions increase heat exhaustion and dehydration risk — session scheduling, shade, cooling zones and mandatory hydration breaks are control measures identified in a risk assessment. Coaches should always check weather forecasts before outdoor sessions and have a written protocol for extreme conditions as part of their Emergency Action Plan.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For questions on hypothermia, always include the 'do nots' — no hot bath, no hot water bottle, do not rub body parts. These are specific to the specification and earn marks. For dehydration questions, remember that thirst is a late sign of dehydration, not an early warning — performers should drink before they feel thirsty. For any 'compare' question on these three conditions, the distinguishing factor is temperature: hypothermia (below 35°C, cold cause), heat exhaustion (38°C or above, hot cause), dehydration (fluid loss, relevant in both hot and cold conditions).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Hypothermia (below 35°C) is treated by removing wet clothing, wrapping in blankets covering the head and giving a warm sugary non-alcoholic drink; never use a hot bath, hot water bottle or rub body parts.
  • Heat exhaustion (38°C or above) is caused by strenuous activity, hot conditions and insufficient fluid intake; treat by moving to a cool place, cooling the skin and drinking plenty of water.
  • Dehydration is caused by fluid loss during exercise and is treated with water and rehydration sachets; symptoms include thirst, fatigue, dark yellow urine and dry mouth, and it is directly linked to heat exhaustion and diabetes.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a performer suffering from hypothermia should not be warmed using a hot bath or hot water bottle.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks. Basic point (1 mark): a hot bath or hot water bottle must not be used to treat hypothermia. Reason (2 marks): rapid heat causes blood vessels near the skin surface to dilate (vasodilate) suddenly. Further development (3 marks): this causes cold blood from the periphery — the arms, legs and skin surface — to rush back to the core all at once, which can cause dangerous cardiac complications and a sudden further drop in core temperature. Warming must therefore be gradual and gentle. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the causes and treatment of dehydration in sport. Give an example of when rehydration sachets would be more appropriate than water alone.
practice_questions.marks: Cause (1 mark): dehydration is caused by loss of bodily fluids — primarily through sweating during exercise — that are not replaced. Treatment (2 marks): drink plenty of water as the first-line treatment (1 mark); use rehydration sachets to restore fluid and electrolyte balance in cases of significant fluid loss (1 mark). Example (1 mark): rehydration sachets would be more appropriate than water alone after a marathon or long-distance endurance event where significant sweating has caused both fluid and electrolyte depletion — replacing water alone without electrolytes can dilute blood sodium and cause hyponatraemia. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A junior football team trains on an exposed pitch on a cold, wet January afternoon. The coach notices that two players are showing signs of hypothermia, and later in the session a third player complains of feeling thirsty and dizzy.

practice_questions.marks:

Prevention discussed with at least two specific measures for future sessions — e.g. mandatory warm kit policy, weather checks before training, drink breaks built into the session plan, risk assessment for cold-weather training. At least one contrast — e.g. the session plan alone cannot prevent all environmental conditions, but an Emergency Action Plan ensures the response is immediate when incidents occur.
Secure (3–4 marks): Both conditions addressed with treatment and some prevention.
Developing (2 marks): One condition treated adequately, prevention vague.
Emerging (1 mark): One relevant point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Three environmental medical conditions — hypothermia, heat exhaustion and dehydration — are all linked to external factors that coaches can influence through planning and preparation.

Evaluate the extent to which effective planning and risk assessment by a coach can prevent these three conditions from occurring during outdoor sport.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A well-structured evaluation arguing that planning reduces risk significantly — risk assessments identify weather hazards, appropriate clothing policies prevent hypothermia, mandatory hydration breaks and water provision prevent dehydration, session scheduling in cooler periods reduces heat exhaustion risk, and Emergency Action Plans ensure rapid response when conditions deteriorate. Counter-arguments then challenge the extent of control: weather is unpredictable, performers arrive with pre-existing dehydration or inadequate kit, coaches cannot control individual hydration habits, and some environmental conditions deteriorate suddenly during a session. A clear, substantiated judgement is reached about what planning can realistically achieve versus what remains outside the coach's control.
Secure (5–6 marks): Arguments on both sides with some application to the scenario and a partial judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): Mainly lists preventive measures without counter-argument or clear judgement.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points with no evaluation. [8 marks]
